📌 Blind Signing: Why Approving What You Can’t Read Is Dangerous

Main Points
⏺ Your wallet sometimes asks you to sign data it cannot decode
⏺ You see a hash or raw hex instead of clear actions
⏺ This post explains why blind signing is risky and how to avoid it


1⃣ Core Idea — Blind signing means approving a transaction or message without a readable summary of what it actually does.
2⃣ Why It Exists — Some smart contracts are complex, and hardware wallets or apps can’t always parse them, so they show only a hash.
3⃣ Example — You expect to claim a reward, but the hidden payload is a token approval or a transfer of your NFTs to someone else.
4⃣ Risk Surface — Phishing sites rely on this: once you sign, the transaction is valid and usually can’t be reversed.
5⃣ Practical Rule — Keep blind signing off by default, use wallets with transaction simulation, and never sign on a site you reached from a DM or ad.
Final Thoughts

A signature is not a formality — it is your consent. If your wallet can’t tell you what you’re approving, assume the worst and stop.

Mitchnick described current interest as “the highest we’ve seen at any point”, pointing to continued demand among wealthy individuals and institutional Bitcoin holders. He identified “security and peace of mind” as the main reasons investors request the service, particularly those seeking alternatives to managing private keys and maintaining large cryptocurrency balances in personal wallets.

➡️ Through in-kind conversions, eligible investors transfer existing Bitcoin into the ETF structure and receive shares representing their investment. DOWN THE RABBIT HOLE — WHAT ARE WE FEEDING OUR GROWTH?

🐇 🍄 🗝️ 👑 ♠️♥️

Do you remember Alice in Wonderland?

Most of us met Alice as children. We remember the White Rabbit, the Cheshire Cat, the Mad Hatter, and the Queen of Hearts. We remember a little girl who fell down a rabbit hole into a world where nothing made sense.

But what if we read that story again through the eyes of faith?

Alice enters Wonderland curious, trusting that the world around her must have some order. Instead, she encounters confusion, contradictions, and authority that demands obedience without offering wisdom.

Does any of that sound familiar?

We live in a world where voices compete for our attention. Some speak with confidence but little truth. Some use fear to control. Some invite us to follow the next rabbit down the next hole, promising that one more discovery will finally explain everything.

And sometimes, while trying to understand the world, we forget to examine what is happening to us.

Remember how Alice grew and shrank depending on what she ate or drank?

I see a picture of our spiritual lives in that.

What are we consuming?

Fear can diminish our courage. Bitterness can shrink our compassion. Pride can make us feel enormous while leaving our understanding painfully small. Endless speculation can occupy our minds until we have little room left for peace.

But God’s Word nourishes a different kind of growth.

Prayer strengthens us. Humility steadies us. Truth gives us roots. Trials, surrendered to God, can deepen our faith instead of destroying it.

“Desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby.” — 1 Peter 2:2 (KJV)

Yet here is something important: not every season in which we feel small means we are backsliding.

Sometimes God is teaching us dependence. Sometimes the valley is the classroom. Sometimes we are being pruned so that we can bear more fruit.

Spiritual maturity is not measured by how powerful we appear, how many secrets we think we’ve uncovered, or how loudly we challenge the world.

It is measured in the fruit we bear.

And then there is the Queen of Hearts.

“Off with their heads!”

Everyone trembles before her threats. Her commands are loud, but loudness is not righteousness. Her title gives her authority, but not wisdom.

How often do we confuse power with truth? Popularity with righteousness? Certainty with discernment?

Alice’s turning point comes when she begins to see through the spectacle. She no longer accepts nonsense simply because it is delivered from a throne.

And faith can give us courage to do likewise—not to assume every suspicion is true, but to test what we hear against what is good, honest, and real.

“Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.” — 1 Thessalonians 5:21 (KJV)

Here is the part that stays with me.

Alice changes size throughout the story. But the change that matters most cannot be measured in inches.

She grows in courage.

She learns to ask questions. She stops letting fear decide what is real. She begins to recognize that what once intimidated her may not deserve the power she gave it.

Perhaps that’s the question Wonderland leaves us with.

Are we growing in faith—or only growing in information?

Are we learning discernment—or becoming dependent on whoever claims to know the way?

Are we feeding our spirits with truth—or swallowing whatever the world puts before us?

We may not choose every rabbit hole we encounter. But we can choose what we consume while we’re there.

And when the world grows louder, the answer is not always to chase another voice.

Sometimes it is to return to the One whose voice never changes.

The goal is not to become the biggest person in Wonderland.

It is to become rooted enough in Christ that Wonderland no longer determines our size.

Stay grounded. Test the voices. Guard what feeds your spirit.

And grow in the direction of the Light.

A Prayer
Father, guard our hearts and sharpen our discernment. Teach us to seek Your truth, not the world’s noise, and to grow in faith and courage. In Jesus’ name, amen.

Europe’s winter energy strategy now depends on mild weather. Gas storage stood at 72% on October 1, well below the EU’s 90% target, and the Iran war has added more than €127 billion to the region’s energy import bill.

A stress test of a cold winter with tight global LNG supplies shows European reserves ending the season barely 10% full, even after a painful 15% cut in demand. Germany’s stocks could run out by March. Europe has little room left for another disruption.

Governments have committed almost €35 billion to cushion the shock. Much of that support is poorly targeted and encourages fossil-fuel consumption, Bloomberg reports. It softens prices without fixing the shortage behind them.

Replacing Russian supplies with American imports has also handed Washington leverage. Earlier this year, Trump threatened a diesel export ban that put half of Europe’s diesel imports at risk. Sweden’s energy minister called trading one dependence for another “problematic.”

German porcelain maker Kahla plans to close after 182 years, with gas accounting for up to 70% of its operating costs. Its 100 workers will be out of jobs long before Europe’s long-term energy strategy pays off.

In the statistics, the closure will register as lower industrial demand for gas. The balance improves because the factory is gone.
